segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: The thing I admire about you, Jacques, is that you operate at a very high level in US science and in Silicon Valley. People trust you and people share information with you. It brings me to the penultimate question, which is government secrecy. If even the illustrious National Academy of Sciences is being shut down, if, as you say, the Pentagon and the intelligence community are so compartmentalized with this UFO secret, then we are being frustrated in even official attempts to get to the truth. If, as you say, Dr. Eric Davis as an individual knows more than Dr. Sean Kirkpatrick inside the Pentagon, what hope is there ever for any kind of meaningful public disclosure of what we're talking about?

segments.speaker: interviewee
segments.text: I think it's understandable that there would be that situation. I'm not the one to blame anybody. I think there is no consensus right now on exactly how this should be addressed. So I think that the first step has been taken, to say that this is a genuine problem. That's not full disclosure, because there are too many areas where we just don't have the answers. And again, the many witnesses that I've spoken to already know that the subject is real, because they have a proof on their property.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Jacques, I just want to explore with you the change that has occurred through the history of your seven Forbidden Science diaries. The earlier Jacques Vallée sometimes sounds as though governments know considerably more than they admit. In the first Forbidden Science volume, for example, you concluded that governments probably knew of the existence and physical reality of the phenomenon and were probably suppressing the data. And then, as your diaries go on, they describe intelligence and military manipulation of scientific debate, and you note your concern that intelligence agencies' interest in paranormal phenomena cannot adequately be explained merely as a response to Soviet research. But the Jacques of Forbidden Science 7 sounds less convinced of the idea that anyone's actually in control. You portray these clusters and these pods of people working on the phenomenon — for example this remote, presumably deep underground military base where Gilbert had this encounter with this non-human being. You surmise in Forbidden Science 7 that maybe nobody's in charge.

segments.speaker: interviewee
segments.text: I really think that nobody is in charge. I think that other countries need to come up with their own data and their own theories. In an epidemic, you cannot say we're going to classify the epidemic — that's what the Chinese tried to do with Covid, to contain it. You cannot do that. And this is the same thing: an atomic war could not be contained to a particular country, because it would wash out over everything else. It would just destroy nature, period, not just one "enemy".

segments.speaker: interviewee
segments.text: The main thing that I've learned, that is disappointing to me, is that the conquest of space is going to be an adversarial pursuit, that we are in competition. But competition can be healthy: I think competition in science between us and China is a good thing, because we move along. The problem is when it becomes conflict, and in space we cannot afford to do it. It's just too complicated, and there are other forces in space and space-time that have something to say about that, and I think that's where the UFO phenomenon comes in. As much as… there is a need for classified programs. As a citizen in good standing I have no right to go to the AEC and say I want to know what kind of hydrogen bomb we're making now, or what do we have that's better than the hydrogen bomb. I have no desire to do that, I have no interest in pursuing that. So it's not true that we all can have access to everything. The problem, as Dr. Travis Taylor was saying, is that there are too many overlapping classified things from those 14 US intelligence agencies that cannot be adjudicated together, and nobody has the clearance to get all that together.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Do you think President Donald Trump knows?

segments.speaker: interviewee
segments.text: I don't know. I respect the fact that the White House has listed this problem as something to be opened up. Once it's opened up — you can see the list of universities now in the US, including Stanford, Harvard, Columbia and others, that have courses that touch on UFOs or are dedicated to UFOs. It's a list of about 30 universities where you can get credit for them. So we've moved. That is the disclosure. It's moving, and it will bring up that new generation. At Stanford there have been three generations of scientists: there was Peter A. Sturrock, and then I took over the collections from Peter Sturrock and his notes, and now there's Dr. Garry Nolan, and I'm trying to assist Dr. Nolan wherever I can in bringing that data to his doorstep so that it can be moved ahead.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: I appreciate that there is a genuine national security concern about not revealing something about the UAP secrets that gives potential foreign adversaries, Russia, China, whoever, any kind of advantage. Do you think, though, Dr. Jacques Vallée, that we could at least be told that non-human intelligences are engaging with this planet, and not in any way jeopardize that national security concern?

segments.speaker: interviewee
segments.text: I think we should, yes. I think we could. And we should, because that would match what many people, if they've taken the time to read the data, must already know.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: You probably more than anyone, Jacques, have done the most, I think, to raise public awareness with the books you've written, the diaries you've kept, the public appearances you've made, of the fact that this is an issue that deserves scientific investigation. You call Forbidden Science 7 your final report. Are you really not going to keep your diaries from now on? Because I suspect your diaries from now on will be the very most interesting ones, Jacques Vallée. Will you be publishing whatever you're recording in your diaries on future occasions?

segments.speaker: interviewee
segments.text: I trust and hope and pray that this is not the end. Now, I think one of the tests of stupidity is when you keep doing the same thing when the situation changes. We know those things are real, there is a phenomenon, so now my role needs to change. I'm not going anywhere, but I'm going to be more active now, as I can: I've been at this a long time, I know where some of the important things are and who was managing it, and I can bring that forward. Most of that is unclassified. I gave a talk in Italy at the Sol Foundation meeting a couple of years ago about a case from 1966 where a physicist is driving through a forest and he sees something that is developing energy that he calculates to exceed the energy of a nuclear power plant.
